Module 6

Managing Data and Business Intelligence

Every order, payment, delivery, and service interaction depends on data. Learn how to make that data trustworthy, organize it in useful structures, and turn it into decisions you can defend. Then connect the work to Porter's five forces and the value chain.

Learn by making the decisions

Work through short lessons and practice immediately. Cases reveal their debriefs after you answer every decision. Sorting, matching, diagrams, and walkthroughs explain the reasoning, and the SQL and spreadsheet labs execute what you type.

  1. Trace the data. Identify sources, transformations, quality problems, and responsible uses.
  2. Model and query it. Build your understanding of keys, relationships, normalization, and business questions.
  3. Choose the repository. Compare operational systems, warehouses, document stores, and lakes by their workloads.
  4. Make the strategy connection. Examine all five forces, locate specific value-chain work, and defend one initiative.
  5. Test your understanding. Finish with 32 new situations scored by objective. Completion records persist in this browser; activity answers reset on reload.

All practice organizations and numerical exhibits are hypothetical. The module follows the supplied Chapter 6 learning objectives 6.1–6.3. Applications 6.4–6.5 extend them into strategy practice. Plan several study sessions; use the contents menu to return to a section.

Final challenge

Thirty-two new situations ask you to choose and explain. Answer all questions, then score to see results by objective. The business situations are hypothetical; use missed questions to choose your next review section.

Continue the practice. Choose an everyday process and sketch its data flow. Name the entities, propose useful keys, write one query question, and explain a data improvement using a force and a value-chain activity.

Reading basis. Supplied Chapter 6, learning objectives 6.1–6.3: strategic data management; relational databases and data warehouses; non-relational databases and data lakes. Framework applications draw on Porter’s strategy concepts. All practice figures are invented; vendor prices, rankings, and chapter forecasts are not presented as current facts.
